scenarios.title: Add IPv6 without losing working IPv4
scenarios.summary: Add a manually chosen IPv6 address alongside an existing IPv4 connection.
scenarios.objective: Give ens3 one unused IPv6 primary address in 2001:db8:110::/64, with the correct /64 prefix. Do not use a supplied peer or router address, or the subnet-router anycast address. Provide a usable simulated IPv6 path to the local peer 2001:db8:110::20 through ens3. An IPv6 default is not required for this local task. Keep the complete working IPv4 configuration unchanged: both interface Up states and IPv4 addresses, all IPv4 routes and IPv4 nameservers. Keep ens4’s IPv6 primary address and every supplied 2001:db8:140::/64 management-route entry unchanged.
steps: Understand the task, investigate the supplied configuration, repair only the requested state and verify the complete handover.
hints: Use the supplied ens3 IPv6 LAN prefix and inspect current IPv6 addresses before adding anything. IPv4 configuration is separate.
An address already used by a supplied peer is not an unused choice. Use the /64 written in the task; IPv6 has no broadcast address.
Use the disclosed ip -6 address add form on ens3, then check both the local path and all preservation requirements.
scenarios.explanation: IPv4 and IPv6 can coexist on ens3. A correct manual primary belongs to the supplied /64 and differs from known peers and the excluded subnet-router anycast address. A local IPv6 peer needs no default route. Adding only the requested primary leaves the separate IPv4 and management state intact.
scenarios.simplifications: Bounded in-process Linux host model: supplied documentation/ULA IPv6 primaries and scoped gateways, separate static main tables, one manual primary per interface and explicit positive IPv6 metrics. No RA/SLAAC/DHCPv6/DAD/NDP, multiple addresses, policy routing, real packets, reverse-path validation, AAAA/NSS or boot persistence. /127–/128 host assignments and subnet-router anycast are activity exclusions, not universal IPv6 rules. Remove this interface’s gateway routes before deleting its primary: a conservative simulator restriction. No host commands or configuration changes.

scenarios.title: Find the interface behind a link-local next hop
scenarios.summary: Choose the correct device for a link-local gateway and find a route that overrides a default.
scenarios.objective: Make the preferred IPv6 default use fe80::1 on ens3, the application link. The same numeric link-local address on ens4 identifies a different router. Provide usable simulated IPv6 paths to 2001:db8:190::80 and 2001:db8:190::90 through ens3. Inspect more-specific routes as well as defaults. Keep both interfaces’ IPv6 primary addresses unchanged; the local peer 2001:db8:110::20 must remain reachable through ens3. Keep the complete working IPv4 configuration unchanged: both interface Up states and IPv4 addresses, all IPv4 routes and IPv4 nameservers. Keep ens4’s IPv6 primary address and every supplied 2001:db8:140::/64 management-route entry unchanged.
steps: Understand the task, investigate the supplied configuration, repair only the requested state and verify the complete handover.

example_actions.input: ip -6 route replace default via fe80::1 dev ens3 metric 100
ip -6 route del 2001:db8:590::80/128 via fe80::1 dev ens4 metric 10

solution: host-action {"kind":"Command","input":"ip -6 route replace default via fe80::1 dev ens3 metric 100"}
host-action {"kind":"Command","input":"ip -6 route del 2001:db8:190::80/128 via fe80::1 dev ens4 metric 10"}
hints: Inspect the IPv6 table. A link-local next hop is an address plus a device, not an address alone.
Compare the /128 for the failing application with the default. The longest matching prefix wins before metric.
The task permits removing or correctly repairing the bad host route; keep the supplied management-prefix entries and both existing IPv6 primaries.
scenarios.explanation: Changing an IPv4 default cannot repair IPv6. ens3 and ens4 each have a distinct router named fe80::1 in their link-local scope. A correct IPv6 default must select the application link, and a lingering wrong /128 can still override it. Verify both destinations and preserve the more-specific management route.

scenarios.title: Complete a protected dual-stack server handover
scenarios.summary: Repair a combined IPv6 incident while preserving working IPv4 and management configuration.
scenarios.objective: Repair ens3 with one unused primary IPv6 address in 2001:db8:110::/64 and the correct prefix. Retain a usable local path to 2001:db8:110::20 through ens3. Make the preferred IPv6 default use fe80::1 on ens3. Both 2001:db8:190::80 and 2001:db8:190::90 must have usable simulated paths through ens3. Investigate the existing address and every matching route. Any unused supported address and positive preferred metric are accepted when the complete requested state holds. Keep the complete working IPv4 configuration unchanged: both interface Up states and IPv4 addresses, all IPv4 routes and IPv4 nameservers. Keep ens4’s IPv6 primary address and every supplied 2001:db8:140::/64 management-route entry unchanged.
steps: Understand the task, investigate the supplied configuration, repair only the requested state and verify the complete handover.

example_actions.input: ip -6 route del 2001:db8:790::90/128 via fe80::2 dev ens3 metric 5
ip -6 route replace default via fe80::1 dev ens3 metric 100

solution: host-action {"kind":"Command","input":"ip -6 route del 2001:db8:190::90/128 via fe80::2 dev ens3 metric 5"}
host-action {"kind":"Command","input":"ip -6 route replace default via fe80::1 dev ens3 metric 100"}
hints: Inspect ip -6 address show and ip -6 route show; keep the working IPv4 configuration unchanged. Compare every field with the supplied task.
The simulator requires removing ens3 gateway routes before changing its exact old IPv6 primary. Retain the separate ens4 management route.
After correcting the primary and preferred default, inspect any remaining /128 entry for its actual device and next hop. Test both applications and the local peer.
scenarios.explanation: This handover combines address-family isolation, prefix correctness, longest-prefix selection and scoped next-hop reasoning. Correct the exact IPv6 faults without changing working IPv4, preserve the independent management route/address, and verify all requested current outcomes. Different supported unused addresses, positive preferred metrics and equivalent route repairs can satisfy the task.
